aliases.name: Boto cor-de-rosa
aliases.meaning: 'Pink boto'; the Amazon river dolphin in its mythical aspect

aliases.name: Boto
aliases.meaning: Common name for Inia geoffrensis, the Amazon river dolphin

description.summary: A shapeshifting being of Amazonian Brazilian folklore that lives by day as a pink river dolphin (boto cor-de-rosa) and emerges at night, especially during festivals, in the form of a tall, handsome, white-clad man who seduces women and lures the unwary into the underwater realm of Encante.
description.full: The Encantado is a class of shapeshifting being central to the folklore of the Brazilian Amazon. By day the Encantado lives as a boto cor-de-rosa, the Amazon river dolphin (Inia geoffrensis); at night, especially during festas (festivals) along the Amazon and its tributaries, it transforms into a tall, handsome, well-dressed man — typically wearing white and a hat to conceal his blowhole — who seduces women, fathers children, and may carry the unwary into Encante, an underwater paradise from which there is no easy return. The legend functions in part as a culturally accepted explanation for the unwanted, scandalous, or unaccountable pregnancies of women in remote river communities. Killing or eating a boto is held to bring lasting bad luck. The figure synthesizes Indigenous Amazonian (Tupi-Guarani) traditions of river-spirits with Portuguese-Catholic narrative forms, and is one of the most widely recognized supernatural figures in northern Brazil. The Wikipedia article on Boto cites Juliette Wood's 'Fantastic Creatures in Mythology and Folklore' (Bloomsbury, 2018, p. 62) as the standard scholarly reference for the legend.

etymology.origin: Portuguese 'encantado', past participle of 'encantar' ('to enchant'), used in Brazilian Amazonian Portuguese as a noun for an enchanted being.
etymology.meaning: 'Encantado' literally means 'enchanted one'; 'boto cor-de-rosa' means 'pink boto', the dolphin's mythic aspect.
etymology.first_use: Long-standing oral tradition in Amazonian Brazil; documented in 19th- and 20th-century Brazilian folklore studies.

related_phenomena.name: Boto (Amazon river dolphin)
related_phenomena.description: The biological species (Inia geoffrensis) on which the legend is grounded.

related_phenomena.name: Selkie
related_phenomena.description: Scottish folkloric seal-people who shift between animal and human form; structurally similar to the Encantado.

related_phenomena.name: Kelpie
related_phenomena.description: Scottish water-horse shapeshifter; comparable role as a seducer and drowner.

features.description: By day appears as Inia geoffrensis, the pink Amazon river dolphin, varying from grey to vivid pink as it ages.
By night appears as a tall, charismatic, well-dressed man, typically in white.
In human form he wears a hat at all times in order to hide the blowhole that remains on the top of his head.
Possesses an extraordinary capacity for charm, dance, and conversation.

physical.morphology: Dual-form being: alternates between the body of the Amazon river dolphin and that of a tall, charismatic human. The blowhole is the diagnostic detail that allegedly persists across the change.

abilities.description: Transforms between dolphin and human forms; the change is most often reported at festivals and at the riverbank.
Charms and seduces human partners — most often women in river-bank communities — at festivals or after sundown.
Can lead lone bathers, children, and lovers to the underwater kingdom of Encante from which they do not return.
Killing or eating an Amazon river dolphin is held to bring severe and lasting bad luck.

behavior.diet: As a dolphin, fish; as a human, the food and drink of festivals.
patterns: Active at night, particularly during local festivals (festa junina, river-festivals)
Targets young women, but also impressionable men in some variants
Most readily encountered along the riverbank or at the edge of a festa
Always wears a hat in human form to conceal the blowhole

range.description: Concentrated in the Brazilian Amazon basin (states of Amazonas, Pará, Acre, Rondônia, Roraima, Amapá), with parallel traditions in adjacent Amazonian regions of Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Venezuela, and the Guianas.

hotspots.name: Mid- and Upper-Amazon riverbank communities

location.description: Riverbank settlements along the main Amazon, Solimões, and Rio Negro corridors of northern Brazil

hotspots.peak_period: Long-standing oral tradition through to present
hotspots.notes: Encantado encounters are reported in association with festas in riverbank towns and villages.

first_recorded.source: Indigenous Amazonian oral traditions; the boto-as-shapeshifter motif is rooted in Tupi-Guarani river-spirit beliefs predating Portuguese contact

origins.cultural_roots: Synthesis of Indigenous Amazonian (Tupi-Guarani) river-spirit traditions with Portuguese-Catholic narrative conventions, developed in the colonial and post-colonial Amazon.
origins.earliest_accounts: Long-standing oral tradition in Amazonian Brazil; recorded in 19th- and 20th-century Brazilian folklore studies, including work by Câmara Cascudo and others.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to a wider Amazonian water-spirit ecology (Cobra Grande, Yara, Mãe-d'Água) and to the global pattern of animal-bride / animal-groom shapeshifters (selkies, kelpies, swan-maidens).

timeline.event: Tupi-Guarani river-spirit traditions establish the conceptual basis for boto-as-shapeshifter narratives
Luís da Câmara Cascudo's 'Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros' (1947) systematizes the figure within Brazilian folklore
Juliette Wood's 'Fantastic Creatures in Mythology and Folklore' (Bloomsbury, 2018) summarizes the boto cor-de-rosa legend in English-language reference literature

history.modern_era: The Encantado remains a living folklore tradition in northern Brazil, invoked in popular music, telenovelas, and tourism, and increasingly enlisted in conservation campaigns aimed at protecting the endangered Amazon river dolphin.

documentary.name: Wood, Fantastic Creatures (2018)
documentary.description: Reference summary of the boto-cor-de-rosa legend in Juliette Wood's 'Fantastic Creatures in Mythology and Folklore' (Bloomsbury, 2018, p. 62).
documentary.analysis: Standard contemporary English-language reference cited by Wikipedia.
documentary.source: Wood, J. (2018), Fantastic Creatures in Mythology and Folklore

paranormal.name: Genuine Amazonian shapeshifter
paranormal.description: Within the lived folklore of the Amazon, the Encantado is treated as a real being whose seductions and abductions explain otherwise unaccountable events along the rivers.
evidence_cited: Cultural narratives of pregnancies attributed to the boto
Local taboos against killing or eating river dolphins

skeptical.name: Social explanatory device for pregnancies
skeptical.description: The legend serves, among other functions, as a culturally accepted cover story for unwanted, premarital, or otherwise stigmatized pregnancies in remote communities.
evidence_cited: Wikipedia (citing Wood, 2018) explicitly notes the use of the legend as a cover for unwanted pregnancies
Contemporary ethnographic reports from Amazonian Brazil

skeptical.name: Conservation-oriented taboo
skeptical.description: Beliefs that killing or eating a boto brings bad luck function as a folkloric conservation mechanism for the endangered Amazon river dolphin.
proponents: Conservation biologists working in the Amazon
evidence_cited: Persistence of strong taboos against harming the boto
Use of the legend in modern conservation messaging

traditions: Festas juninas and other riverbank festivals
stories: A handsome man in white appears at a riverbank festival, dances with a young woman, and disappears at dawn; she later proves to be pregnant
Lone bathers vanish into the river and are said to have been taken to Encante
Hunters who kill river dolphins suffer enduring misfortune
folklore.beliefs: River dolphins are addressed as 'boto', not as 'dolphins', and are not to be killed or eaten; eye contact with a boto at a festival is to be avoided.

cultures: Riberinho (river-bank) communities of mixed Indigenous and Lusophone heritage
indigenous.significance: The Encantado is grounded in Indigenous river-spirit traditions and remains an active part of the cultural and spiritual life of riberinho communities, intersecting with conservation and gender norms.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: The legend is a living tradition rather than an historical curiosity; its use in cover-story narratives can intersect with serious questions of consent and gender violence in local communities, and should be discussed with care.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Brazilian and Indigenous scholars where possible; avoid sensationalizing the figure as a generic 'cryptid'.
